description: We consider outselves a creative team to lead the project «Junior Astronaut Mission Simulator». The goal is to develop an interactive platform that brings astronomy closer to children and fosters their,  interest in space from an early age. Besides,  to build a multidisciplinary team, we are looking for members with an innovative vision, web development skills, and talent for creative storytelling. Anyone interested in joining this initiative should not hesitate to become part of the team.
summary: Base Esperanza: Guardians of Mars is a free, browser-based survival game that teaches maths, physics and chemistry to children aged 6–12. Players are astronauts who must keep a Mars base alive for 30 sols. When an alarm sounds, they run into a room in trouble and solve a real science problem: making oxygen from water, stacking regolith against solar radiation, cleaning dusty solar panels, cleaning CO₂ from the cabin with a MOXIE-type reactor, and watering crops without wasting water. Guessing costs energy and health, so kids learn to calculate before acting. Every crisis is linked to something that really happened in NASA missions (MOXIE, Curiosity, InSight, Apollo 13, Veggie), and the solar storm crisis reads live solar-flare data from NASA DONKI. A roaming robot called Glitch adds suspense and keeps kids engaged. The game runs on phones and PCs, works offline, is fully bilingual (Spanish/English), the costumer needs to log in, and gives teachers a CSV progress report.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Base Esperanza is an educational survival game. A crew must survive 30 sols on Mars until the relief ship arrives. An "event director" launches 5 crises; each one is a hands-on science problem:

1. Oxygen leak (chemistry): electrolysis, 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂.

2. Solar storm (physics): regolith shielding against radiation.

3. Power failure (math/physics): dusty vs. clean solar panels.

4. High CO₂ (chemistry): MOXIE-type reactor, 2 CO₂ → 2 CO + O₂, only inside a safe heat range.

5. Crop at risk (math): proportions of water and nutrients per tray.

Resources are shared: water spent on oxygen is missing later for the crops, so kids learn that decisions have consequences.

DESIGNED FOR KIDS 6–12

Two levels (Grades 1–2 and Grades 3–6), short sentences, emoji-based questions, read-aloud voice, 3 progressive hints (more help = fewer stars), green/red feedback, and a "Why?" explanation after every answer. Big touch buttons with icon + word (USE, JUMP, RUN, FREEZE), a virtual joystick, full-screen mode and a phone-friendly layout. Three clear views: Map (2D), 3D (behind your astronaut) and Eyes (first person). On shared school computers, "Who is playing?" lets each child continue their own mission or start as a new player. The Manual shows every formula (e.g., 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂) plus a Units - and - Symbols glossary (kW, mSv, °C, H₂O, CO₂, 2ⁿ).

REAL NASA SCIENCE

Each crisis shows a short "It really happened!" card: oxygen made from water on the Space Station, the May 2024 solar storm measured by Curiosity on Mars, InSight shut down by dust on its solar panels (2022), Apollo 13's CO₂ filter (1970), and the first lettuce eaten in space (Veggie, 2015). After solving a crisis, kids get a real NASA fact (e.g., MOXIE made 122 g of oxygen in 16 runs). The solar storm crisis reads the last 30 days of solar flares live from NASA DONKI; if there is no internet it says so and never invents data.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

Most science games are quizzes. Here kids explore a 3D base, react to alarms under time pressure, and avoid Glitch, a broken robot that patrols the base (inspired by the suspense of "survival" games, kept kid-friendly). Mistakes have consequences, but kids get a clear explanation instead of a punishment. Teachers get a progress table that can be exported as CSV.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- Single HTML file (HTML, CSS, JavaScript). No install, no login, no server.

- 3D: three.js r160 (MIT), embedded so it works offline; built-in 2D map fallback.

- Sound: Web Audio API (all sounds synthesized in the browser).

- Voice: Web Speech API (read-aloud).

- Data: NASA DONKI API (api.nasa.gov) for live solar flares; cited NASA facts stored in the game.

- Saving: localStorage (progress stays on the device; no personal data is sent anywhere).

- Hosting: GitHub Pages.

USE OF AI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)

Made by Team Killa (no AI): the game concept and survival-suspense mechanics (inspired by Five Nights at Freddy's and R.E.P.O.), game design, levels, the math/physics/chemistry problems, characters and abilities, the space base, the Mars exterior and the environments. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic): English translation, bug fixing, control tuning, mobile adaptation and polishing (simpler kid texts, suspense lighting, NASA fact cards). The team reviewed and play-tested every change. No AI-generated images, video or audio. Disclosed in the code header, the in-game credits and the README.

IMPACT

Free and offline-capable, so it works in schools with weak internet and on cheap phones. Spanish and English widen its reach in Latin America. It turns abstract formulas into survival decisions that kids can feel.
